title: The whole journey
summary: From the Planck length to the edge of the observable universe in about 90 seconds.

steps.caption: The Planck length: about 10⁻³⁵ metres. No experiment can reach this small, so this is an artist's idea, not a measurement.
Fourteen powers of ten where no experiment has found anything at all. This gap is the edge of human knowledge.
A proton, about 1.7 femtometres across. Three quarks swirl inside it, held together by gluons.
A carbon atom is about 150 picometres wide. Almost all of it is empty space. Its nucleus is tens of thousands of times smaller.
DNA is only about 2 nanometres wide. Its twisted ladder of paired bases holds the instructions for building you.
A human skin cell, about 30 micrometres across. You are made of tens of trillions of cells like this one.
You, 1.7 metres tall. From here it is about 35 powers of ten down to the Planck length and about 27 up to the universe.
Earth is about 12,700 kilometres across. Every person who has ever lived has lived on this one small world.
The Sun is about 109 Earths wide. Its light takes about eight minutes to reach us.
The Solar System out to Neptune's orbit: about 9 billion kilometres across. Light needs around eight hours to cross it.
The Milky Way holds hundreds of billions of stars across roughly 100,000 light-years. The Sun is one of them, about 26,000 light-years from the centre.
The observable universe: about 93 billion light-years across. The most distant light we can see left its source over 13 billion years ago.

title: Inside you
summary: Zoom from a whole person into a skin cell, DNA, an atom and the quarks inside a proton.

steps.caption: Start with a person, about 1.7 metres tall. You are about to shrink a very long way.
Zoom into your skin. It is only a couple of millimetres thick, and it is built from living cells.
A skin cell is about 30 micrometres across. Inside it, the nucleus holds your DNA.
DNA: a double helix about 2 nanometres wide. Each of your cells holds around two metres of it, folded up tightly.
A single carbon atom. Its electrons are not tiny planets on tracks. They form a fuzzy cloud showing where each electron is likely to be.
The nucleus of carbon-12: six protons and six neutrons. It is roughly 30,000 times smaller than the atom around it.
Each proton and neutron is itself made of smaller particles called quarks.
Three quarks held together by gluons. Experiments show they are smaller than 10⁻¹⁸ metres, and nobody has ever seen a quark on its own.

title: Our place in space
summary: From a person on Earth out to the observable universe, one step at a time.

steps.caption: You, standing on a headland near Wollongong. Now we zoom out, one giant leap at a time.
Planet Earth, about 12,700 kilometres across. The thin blue edge is the atmosphere that keeps you alive.
The Sun is a star about 109 Earths wide. It holds more than 99 percent of all the mass in the Solar System.
The Solar System out to Neptune's orbit. The planets are tiny specks in a huge, mostly empty space.
A light-year is the distance light travels in a year: nearly 10 trillion kilometres. The nearest star is over four light-years away.
Our home galaxy, the Milky Way. The Sun sits in one of its spiral arms, about 26,000 light-years from the centre.
Galaxies gather into clusters and long filaments, a cosmic web with enormous empty voids between them.
The edge of the observable universe. Because light needs time to travel, looking further away means looking further back in time.
